newsitem.title: USA: Hughes target of bidding war.
newsitem.headline: Hughes target of bidding war.

text.p: Northrop Grumman Corp. and Raytheon Co. both bid $9 billion or more for Hughes Electronics' missile and radar businesses, sources familiar with the bidding said Thursday.

Raytheon reportedly has bid $9 billion for the businesses while Northrop Grumman was said to have offered as much as $500 million more, starting the latest bidding war in the shrinking defence industry.
"Northrop and Raytheon have put in bids," one investment banker familiar with the auction said.
None of the companies would comment.

A deal would be one of the biggest ever in the industry, falling short only of the $14.6 billion takeover of McDonnell Douglas Corp. by Boeing Co. and close in size to Lockheed Martin Corp.'s $9.1 billion acquisition of Loral Corp. last year.

Hughes Electronics shares, which trade separately from the shares of its parent General Motors Corp., rose $2.125 to $63.125 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange while Raytheon and Northrop Grumman both fell.
Raytheon lost $1.25 to $47.50 and Northrop fell $1.375 to $77.875, both on the NYSE.
"I don't think it's necessarily the high bidder that will win," said Paul Nisbet, a defence analyst at JSA Research.

The winner will emerge as the premier firm in the defence electronics business. At stake are Hughes businesses with annual revenues of about $6.2 billion. The assets include missile systems, radar and communications electronics, air traffic control systems and an electro-optical devices unit.
By selling the business, GM's Hughes will be able to focus on more promising areas, such as satellites and DirectTV.
General Motors' desire to avoid a hefty tax bill and the comparative financial strength of Raytheon give it the edge in the auction, analysts said.
"It's more advantageous to Raytheon because it's larger and stronger financially (than Northrop)," Nisbet said.

Analysts said that to avoid paying about $2 billion of capital gains taxes resulting from a cash sale of Hughes, GM wants to load Hughes with up to $5 billion in debt. Hughes currently has only $200 million of debt.
Stock of the acquiring company would make up the balance of the payment. The cost to the acquiring company could be reduced by $1 billion or more if goodwill is classified as tax deductible.

"For Northrop to issue $4 billion to $6 billion in stock they would actually have to issue enough stock to give a majority holding to General Motors, whereas Raytheon would have to give about 30 percent of their holdings (to GM)," Nisbet said.
He added that it was unlikely GM would want to hold a majority interest in Northrop.
In Northrop's favour is a history of bidding above the odds when it wants an acquisition, analysts said.
"It would seem to me that Raytheon can come in lower than Northrop and still get it," Nisbet said.
Northrop has about $3.3 billion in debt with $1.6 billion in shareholder equity.

Raytheon -- even after its agreement this week to buy Texas Instrument Inc.'s defence assets for $2.95 billion -- has about $6.5 billion of debt with about $4.6 billion in stockholder equity, making its debt load lighter relative to Northrop's.

Further giving Raytheon an edge are three non-defence units it could sell for as much as $6 billion to $7 billion, softening the heavy debt load that would come with Hughes, experts said. Northrop has nothing to sell to raise cash.
"I think Raytheon has the upper hand just because of that," said William Fiala, an analyst at brokerage firm Edward Jones. "Their options are almost limitless."
The latest round of mergers and acquisition in the defence industry is a result of continually dwindling U.S. government spending.

Stuart McCutchan, editor of Defence Mergers & Acquisitions, said U.S. government spending on defence has shrunk in real terms every year since 1986. That means companies need to make acquisitions to gain economies of scale needed to remain competitive, he said.
